tasks.short: Tell or walk a customer to the shelf where a product is, asking colleagues when unsure.

steps.what: Customer asks at the till where a product is
Cashier recalls the aisle or searches the item and stock on the till
Cashier radios a floor colleague when the product location is unknown
Floor colleague checks the shelf or stock room and replies
Cashier explains the route or walks the customer to the products

tasks.design: Configure an aisle-bay-shelf field on the item master and fill it from planogram data held in the {OPS_SYSTEM}, so the item search on the {OTHER} point-of-sale till shows location and store stock in one result. Items without a location stay on the radio route, and the cashier flags wrong locations from the same screen.
tasks.previous_blocker: Shelf locations lived in planogram drawings and staff memory, not in the item record the till can search.
tasks.enabler_now: Most till and stock systems accept extra item attributes, and a small integration can copy planogram locations into them nightly.
tasks.still_hard: Promotion displays, seasonal moves and second placements change faster than planogram data; vague descriptions ('the thing for descaling') still need a person.
tasks.human_edge: Reading what the customer actually needs, offering a nearby alternative, and walking someone who is unsure or less mobile to the shelf.

ambition.what: Customers who look up the aisle of an item on the shop's {ECOMMERCE} pages or app before they come in or while in the store.

tasks.altitude: The cashier spends less time on the radio and the same time with the customer; nothing changes in decision rights.

reach.task: Tell customers where rental items and accessories are kept
reach.learn: Whether one location field in the item record serves both shop floor and rental counter.

evidence.claim: Till and stock systems can hold a shelf location as an item attribute and show it in item search.
A large Dutch web shop runs an assistant next to search that asks follow-up questions and compares features, price and delivery.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's question to the customer at the shelf; restocking and planogram changes are outside.
Input contract: item ID, description, aisle, bay and shelf per store, produced by the merchandising team in the {OPS_SYSTEM} planogram; fallback is the radio call to a floor colleague.
Native configuration is tried first: a custom item attribute in the till before any separate app.
Upkeep for the cashier is flagging wrong locations; maintaining planogram data stays with merchandising.
The customer and floor colleague time is outside the cashier's savings.
unknowns: Whether planogram locations are kept per store in a system or only as drawings.
How many questions a cashier gets per shift.
research_questions: What share of location questions are about items on promotion displays or second placements?

already_counted.description: Cashier still explains the route or walks the customer to the shelf.

incremental.description: Cashier flags wrong or missing shelf locations from the till screen.
Merchandising keeps the location field current after planogram changes.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Location data covers only items on fixed planograms; promotion and seasonal items still go to the radio, and the walk to the shelf does not change.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check a returned item against the sale and policy, key the refund or exchange, and sort the item.

steps.what: Customer brings item and receipt and says why it goes back
Cashier finds the original sale by receipt barcode or by searching
Cashier checks returns policy: days since sale, category, proof
Cashier inspects merchandise condition and decides refund, exchange or refusal
Cashier keys return or exchange lines with a reason code
Supervisor approves exception returns with an override at the till
Cashier pays the refund to card or cash and prints the receipt
Cashier tags returned merchandise for restock, damage or supplier return

tasks.design: Configure the return rules (days since sale, excluded categories, refund to original tender) in the {OTHER} point-of-sale return module so the till shows the policy outcome and pre-fills the return lines and refund tender once the sale is found, and only flagged exceptions ask the supervisor for an override on a handheld. The reason code the cashier picks drives the disposition: the till prints a bin label and an integration posts the stock movement or supplier-return line to the {OPS_SYSTEM}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Return rules sat in a printed policy and supervisors' heads, and disposition went on paper tags keyed later by the stock team.
tasks.enabler_now: Point-of-sale return modules hold rule settings and reason codes, and a small integration can turn reason codes into stock movements.
tasks.still_hard: Judging wear, missing parts and signs of use stays a person's call; receipts without a match still need a manual search.
tasks.human_edge: Judging the item's condition, calming an unhappy customer and choosing between exchange and refund when the rule does not fit.

ambition.what: Supplier-return claims raised for every faulty item on the day it comes back, instead of when the damage bin is full.

tasks.altitude: The cashier keeps the judgement on condition but no longer calls the supervisor for routine returns; supervisors see only flagged exceptions.

reach.task: Check in rental items and record damage
reach.learn: Whether the same reason codes and damage tags work for rental returns.

evidence.claim: Point-of-sale return modules support configured return windows, reason codes and supervisor overrides.
In-store returns of non-faulty goods follow the shop's own policy; faulty goods fall under the legal guarantee, with national rules on details.
Finding a sale without a receipt by payment card uses personal data, so GDPR purpose and retention rules apply.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer presenting the item to the item tagged for disposition; supplier claims and restocking are outside.
Input contract: original sale record with sale ID, date, items, prices and tender, produced by the till; fallback for no receipt is a manual search or a store-credit rule.
Native configuration is tried first: the return module's rule and reason-code settings before custom code.
Supervisor and customer time are outside the cashier's savings.
The refund payout itself does not change; integrated card terminals are assumed already in place.
unknowns: Which return rules and limits the shop uses and how often supervisors are called today.
Whether the till already supports lookup by payment card or e-receipt.
research_questions: What share of returns come without a receipt or with a disputed condition?

already_counted.description: Cashier judges the condition of returned merchandise.

incremental.description: Cashier reports policy outcomes that look wrong and corrects mis-coded dispositions.
Retail operations maintains return rules, category exclusions and reason codes.

approvals.approved_version: For flagged exception returns only: return transaction number with refund amount and tender as keyed in s5; any change voids the override.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Shops with many receipt-less or disputed returns keep most manual searching and judgement; disposition saving holds only where the stock system takes reason-code movements.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: At closing, total payments per tender, compare with the till's sales, explain variances and hand over.

steps.what: Cashier prints the till's end-of-period sales report with totals per tender
Cashier counts cash in the drawer by denomination
Cashier totals card terminal slip and vouchers received
Cashier fills the cash-up sheet: counted against expected payments per tender
Cashier traces variances over tolerance in voids, refunds and keyed payments
Supervisor recounts if needed and signs off the closing record
Finance team keys daily sales takings and variance into the ledger

tasks.design: Use the closing screen of the {OTHER} point-of-sale system: it already knows expected payments per tender, takes card totals from the integrated terminal, and the cashier only enters the counted cash, so the variance is computed on the spot. A filtered list of voids, cash refunds and no-sale openings helps trace a variance, the supervisor signs off the closing in the till, and an integration posts the approved daily takings to the {ERP}, with a variance dashboard in {BI} for the store manager.
tasks.previous_blocker: Tills, card terminals and the ledger were not connected, so cash-up sheets and mailed reports tied them together.
tasks.enabler_now: Point-of-sale closing screens show expected totals per payment type and take the counted amount; till-to-ledger integrations are cheap to build.
tasks.still_hard: Counting cash stays physical, and variances from wrong change leave no trace in the till data.
tasks.human_edge: Recounting carefully, explaining what happened during a busy shift and owning the drawer's balance.

ambition.what: A store manager who sees each day's till variances by register and tender the next morning, not at month end.

tasks.altitude: The cashier's closing shrinks to counting and explaining; the supervisor approves in the till instead of on paper.

reach.task: Reconcile store takings with bank deposits and card settlements
reach.learn: Which closing fields the ledger posting needs so finance no longer chases sheets.

evidence.claim: A point-of-sale closing screen shows expected totals per payment type and staff enter the counted amount.
Cash-up sheets and mailed end-of-day reports often tie tills to the ledger; a till-to-ledger integration and variance dashboard replace them.
In the Netherlands, reports of variances per cashier make the tool fit to monitor staff, which needs works council consent.
AI systems that monitor and evaluate staff performance are high-risk under AI Act Annex III; a model scoring cashiers from variances would fall there.

assumptions: Boundary: from the end of the cashier's period to the daily takings posted in the ledger; banking the cash is outside.
Input contract: closing record with register ID, period, expected and counted totals per tender, variance and note, produced by the till; fallback is the cash-up sheet when the till closing is down.
Card terminals are integrated with the till or can be; if not, the cashier still keys the slip total.
Supervisor and finance team time are outside the cashier's savings.
Existing till runtime that already computes expected totals earns no saving.
The variance list and dashboard are deterministic queries, not an AI system; no model scores cashiers.
unknowns: Whether card terminals are integrated with the till in every store.
The variance tolerance and who owns it.
Whether a works council has agreed to per-cashier variance reports.
research_questions: What share of closing variances are traced to till data versus wrong change given?

already_counted.description: Cashier counts cash and explains variances.
Supervisor signs off the closing record in the till.

incremental.description: Cashier handles closing-screen errors and falls back to the sheet when the till is down.
Finance team monitors the ledger posting and fixes failed days.

approvals.approved_version: Register closing record for one register and period, locked at supervisor sign-off; a recount or edit voids it.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Stores whose card terminals are not integrated keep keying slip totals, and busy-shift variances still need long manual tracing.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: At shift start, count the float in the drawer, record it and get more change if short.

steps.what: Supervisor counts the float from the safe into the drawer
Cashier counts the money in the drawer by denomination
Cashier writes the opening count on the paper float sheet
Cashier radios for extra coins or small notes when change is short
Supervisor brings change from the safe and logs the swap

tasks.design: Configure the opening screen of the {OTHER} point-of-sale till so the cashier enters the count per denomination; the till compares it with the float issued and with a minimum per denomination, records cashier and time, and replaces the paper float sheet. When a denomination is below its minimum, a small automation sends a prefilled change request to the supervisor's handheld for the cashier to confirm.
tasks.previous_blocker: Float records lived on paper sheets because tills only tracked sales, not the cash handed over at opening.
tasks.enabler_now: Point-of-sale register opening screens take a counted float, and a simple rule on denomination counts can trigger a notification.
tasks.still_hard: The physical count stays; coin counting machines or cash recyclers need capital spend and are not assumed.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting a short or wrongly packed float before the first customer and owning the drawer from that moment.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; the cashier starts the shift a few minutes sooner.

reach.role: gambling change person or booth cashier
reach.task: Count the booth bank at shift start
reach.learn: Whether the same per-denomination minimums and change requests fit a cash booth.

evidence.claim: Point-of-sale systems can record an opening float per register and compare it with what was issued.
In the Netherlands, recording opening differences per cashier can make the till a tool fit to monitor staff, which needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the float leaving the safe to the cashier ready to trade; banking and safe counts are outside.
Input contract: float issue with register ID, amount and denomination breakdown, produced by the supervisor at the safe; fallback is the paper float sheet.
Native configuration is tried first: the till's register-opening screen before any separate app.
The supervisor's safe and change runs stay as they are and are outside the cashier's savings.
The count itself does not get faster; only the recording and the change request change.
s3 is part of keeping balance sheets, which sibling task 41-2011.00:2414 covers; its saving is counted there, so s3 keeps its full time here.
unknowns: Whether the till supports an opening count per denomination.
Whether supervisors carry a handheld that can receive requests.
research_questions: How often does a cashier run short of change in the first hour of a shift?

already_counted.description: Cashier confirms the prefilled change request.

incremental.description: Cashier corrects mistyped opening counts and uses the paper fallback when the till is down.
Store manager keeps denomination minimums per register current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Stores without handhelds keep the radio call, and cashiers who recount after a typo lose part of the recording saving.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The cashier keeps the counter, the cash count and the customer conversation; less time goes to paper sheets, radio calls and supervisor overrides.
reach: Counter and rental clerk check-in of returned items
Accounts receivable reconciliation of store takings
skills_to_grow: Explaining a variance from till data
Judging returned goods consistently against reason codes
Spotting wrong item data and reporting it
role.ambitious_version: A cashier who closes a register in minutes, sees the day's variances and flags item and policy data problems that the shop then fixes for every till.
